title: Cats: Invasive Species?
summary: Josh and Chuck open with comic strip banter (Nancy, Sally Forth, Doonesbury, Beetle Bailey), then examine whether domestic cats are an invasive species. They cover cat domestication in the Middle East and Cyprus about 12,000 years ago tied to grain stores and mice, the mutualism of the cat-human relationship, and the difference between pet, outdoor, and feral cats. They cite estimates of birds and mammals killed by cats each year in the US (a 2013 Smithsonian and US Fish and Wildlife Service study), species extinctions linked to cats (including the Stephens Island wren after the cat Tibbles arrived), and cat-spread toxoplasmosis and rabies. They discuss feral cat populations, the role of urban coyotes in suppressing feral cats, and solutions: indoor-only cats, trap-neuter-return (TNR) programs and high-intensity TNR, the lethal alternative favored by some biologists, Australia's poison traps, and leash or licensing laws. They note the scientific debate between the two sides. The episode closes with a listener mail about the Greenbrier bunker.

segments.title: Opening banter on comic strips
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck reminisce about classic comic strips such as Nancy, Sally Forth, Doonesbury, Beetle Bailey and Brenda Starr before introducing the topic.

segments.title: Cats as an invasive species: framing and origins
segments.summary: The hosts introduce cats as a widely held invasive species concern among conservation biologists and explain the scientific divide. They trace domestic cat origins to Middle Eastern wildcats (Felis silvestris), domestication about 12,000 years ago tied to grain stores and rodents, and fossil evidence from Cyprus and a buried cat.

segments.title: Cat-human mutualism
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whether the cat-human relationship is commensal or mutualistic, concluding it is mutualistic because both species benefit.

segments.title: Pet, outdoor, and feral cats; semi-domestic status
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish pet cats, outdoor cats and feral cats, note that feral cats cause the main problems, contrast them with invasive pythons and feral dogs, and say cats are considered semi-domesticated.

segments.title: Cats hunting wildlife and kill estimates
segments.summary: They discuss why cats bring home prey and give estimates from a study of cat-caused bird and mammal deaths in the US, saying feral cats kill about three times as many as pet cats. They also cite species extinctions linked to rodents and cats.

segments.title: Tibbles and the Stephens Island wren
segments.summary: The story of the cat Tibbles, who arrived on Stephens Island off New Zealand in the 1890s, and the flightless Stephens Island wren's extinction, which they note is hard to verify. They say biologists' estimates tend to be conservative.

segments.title: Disease and toxoplasmosis
segments.summary: Cats spread disease including rabies and toxoplasmosis, which reproduces only in the cat gut and can harm many warm-blooded animals. They note the indirect effects on predators such as hawks and owls.

segments.title: Pet cat numbers and feral cat population
segments.summary: They estimate about 86 million US pet cats, a large share of which roam outdoors, and say feral populations may be about 30 million or possibly close to 80 million. They discuss the indoor-only cat recommendation and litter box subscription services.

segments.title: Predators, urban coyotes and feral cats
segments.summary: Adult feral cats have few natural predators. A 2013 Ohio study suggested urban coyotes keep feral cat numbers down, and some bird and small mammal populations are rebounding as a result.

segments.title: Trap-neuter-return (TNR) and high-intensity TNR
segments.summary: They explain TNR, which began in the late 1990s: feral cats are trapped, spayed or neutered, ear-tipped and released, rather than euthanized. A 2019 study found high-intensity TNR reduced feral cat populations and preventable cat deaths. They note the high kitten mortality and that low-intensity TNR may be worse than nothing.

segments.title: Lethal control, Australia poison traps, and policy options
segments.summary: They discuss the lethal alternatives some biologists favor, Australia's poison traps that cats ingest through grooming, public reaction, and policy ideas such as cat licensing and leash laws. They say the question is one of will.

segments.title: Debate between biologists and cat advocates
segments.summary: They describe the public dispute between wildlife biologists and cat advocates over the TNR studies, including claims that cats mostly prey on weak or old animals and accusations of bad science.

segments.title: Listener mail: Greenbrier bunker
segments.summary: Listener Greg from Columbus shares details of his tour of the Greenbrier bunker, including its blast doors, facilities, congressional medicine stocks, and the Secret Service drill to reach the bunker in eleven minutes.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and sign off, with a mail address and credits.
